claims.text: Đơn Hàng's delivery-metrics.md takes four measures from a long-running research program on software delivery (DORA metrics): deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service.
claims.source_hint: docs/team/delivery-metrics.md lines 3-5 and table lines 12-17 at stage-4

claims.text: Deployment frequency and lead time for changes measure throughput; change failure rate and time to restore service measure stability.
claims.source_hint: DORA four key metrics description (throughput vs stability); delivery-metrics.md table lines 12-17

claims.text: The DORA metrics are read together: more deploys a week while the change failure rate rises is not progress, nor is a low failure rate from deploying once a month, since each rare release bundles many changes.
claims.source_hint: docs/team/delivery-metrics.md section 'Đọc bốn số cùng nhau'

claims.text: delivery-metrics.sh counts as a deploy each commit touching envs/production that adds a newTag: sha- line, except reverts and the repository's first commit (lines 81-85).
claims.source_hint: scripts/devops/delivery-metrics.sh lines 74-88 at stage-4; git-log/git-show docs

claims.text: A commit whose subject starts with Revert is counted as one failed change; the undone commit id is read from the body line 'This reverts commit <id>.' and restore time = revert time minus that deploy's time, in minutes.

Line 88 lists commits touching envs/production oldest first (--reverse) with commit time in seconds (%ct); lead time = promotion commit time minus the time of the app commit the sha- tag names (lines 86-87).

The script takes the promotion commit's time as the moment the change reached production and the revert commit's time as when production was back on a working version; delivery-metrics.md defines both from these commits.
Captured output at stage-4: 10 deploys, 0.8 a week; lead time median 51.5 hours; change failure rate 2 of 10, 20%; time to restore median 117.5 minutes (45 and 190).

Lead time and restore time are reported as medians (middle value; for an even count the mean of the two middle ones: 29.0 and 74.0 give 51.5, 45 and 190 give 117.5) so one change that waited long does not pull lead time up.

The history is a made-up quarter with fixed dates, so the output is the same on every run; the script needs no cluster and can be run from a terminal at the repository root (line 5 re-runs it inside the lab container).
claims.source_hint: delivery-metrics.sh lines 2-10; scripts/lab-run.sh; STAGE.md capture mode --all list

claims.text: delivery-metrics.md names three sources: config repository (deploys, reverts), application repository (commit times), and written failure records for failures fixed without a revert; the script reads only git log, so only the first two.

A failure fixed by a forward fix or a setting changed on the cluster leaves no revert, so the history counts that deploy as good; a missing record makes the change failure rate lower than it really is.
Time to restore runs from the failed deploy: from Git history, to the revert; from a written record, to the time it gives for service being back, which is more precise when the record has it.

The metrics describe the delivery system (pipeline, review, tests, how deploys are done), not people; used to rank developers they get gamed, e.g. by splitting one change into many deploys or not writing failure records.
claims.source_hint: delivery-metrics.md section 'Không dùng để đánh giá cá nhân'

claims.text: When asked for per-developer lead time, report the team's median and where changes wait; when deploys rise with change failure rate, do not call it progress, look at reverted changes first, and check next quarter whether the rise holds, since few deploys make the rate swing.

Without the second revert (the 190-minute one) the script would report 10 deploys (0.8 a week), lead time median unchanged at 51.5 hours, change failure rate 1 of 10 (10%), time to restore 45 minutes.
claims.source_hint: delivery-metrics.sh lines 53-60 and 72-98 applied to the history without that revert

claims.text: Lead time for changes starts at a commit, not at the first idea for a feature.
claims.source_hint: DORA definition of lead time for changes; glossary lead-time-for-changes

claims.text: Trade-offs: records cost someone writing one for each failure not fixed by a revert; history-only numbers can be gamed by fixing forward instead of reverting, records by not writing them; rare bundled releases make the failed change harder to find.
